2090-peach-blossom-shangri-la-tao-hua-yu:
Tao Yuanming's famous Chinese tale, given here in English and in the Chinese original, tells of a fisherman of Wuling. He follows a stream past a grove of peach trees in full bloom. Petals fall thick on the water as he presses on. Tao Yuanming wrote in the fourth and fifth centuries, when China was torn by war and division.

Beyond the grove he finds a hidden valley where people live in peace, apart from the world outside. The short tale became the model for every later Chinese vision of a lost paradise, and its name still means a place of quiet refuge. The hidden valley's peace contrasts sharply with the fisherman's own troubled world outside.
61740-lolo-ma-or-two-years-in-cannibal-l:
Henry Britton, author of Fiji in 1870, published Loloma, or Two Years in Cannibal-land in Melbourne and London in 1884. He dedicated the tale to J B Thurston, first colonial secretary of Fiji. The preface states the aim in plain terms.

Britton hoped to keep a record of old Fijian manners, customs, lore, and beliefs before they faded. He drew on the Rev. Jesse Carey, a missionary who asked native men across the islands to write essays on the past. Fifty men replied, and their work fed the tale. Britton calls the Fijians the most numerous race in the South Pacific and insists his facts on their life are strict and true.
66057-the-tale-of-genji:
Lady Murasaki wrote The Tale of Genji, here in Arthur Waley's translation. Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York put it out in 1925. Waley gives the book to Beryl de Zoete on the title page. A preface, a list of the chief persons, and family tables open it. The chapters begin with Kiritsubo, the hero's mother.

The Broom-Tree, Utsusemi, Yugao, and Murasaki follow in the contents. The Saffron-Flower, the Festival of Red Leaves, and the Flower Feast come next. Aoi, the ninth chapter, closes this first volume of the tale. Genji is the son of an emperor and his concubine Kiritsubo. Princess Aoi is his wife, and Fujitsubo his father's consort, whom he loves. Murasaki is a child he adopts, who becomes his second wife. Waley gives the great Japanese romance in English dress.
76974-at-home-in-fiji:
Gordon Cumming wrote a travel book on her stay in Fiji, in a new edition issued in New York in 1882. She had sailed by way of Sydney and the Blue Mountains, and she writes as a guest in island homes. Her book is full of the daily round of life in the tropics.

Chapters treat Levuka and its harbour, coral reefs, church life, and the brewing of yangona. She rides the Rewa river, sleeps in a native house, and marks feasts, weddings, and funerals. King Thakombau and the work of the missions both figure large. Readers in Britain and America got from her a warm, close view of Fiji as she found it.
britannica-1911-awaji:
Awaji is a Japanese island at the eastern entrance of the Inland Sea. The island runs thirty-two miles long and up to sixteen miles broad. Its area is 218 square miles, and its people number about 190,000. The Naruto channel parts it from Shikoku to the south, where tides can drive a remarkable rushing current.

Tradition holds Awaji the first of the Japanese islands created by the gods Izanagi and Izanami, a claim the entry records with its scenery. Its highest peak rises to 1,998 feet, and another summit is praised as most picturesque. The island is also noted for a peculiar local pottery. Beauty, sacred origin, and craft give this short entry its three points of interest.
britannica-1911-cherrapunji:
Cherrapunji is a village in the Khasi hills district of Assam, noted for rain on a scale found nowhere else in the known record. The entry calls it the place with the heaviest known rainfall in the world. In 1861 it registered a total of 905 inches. Its annual average stands at 458 inches, a figure far beyond a wet climate in the usual sense.

The cause lies in the site, and the entry explains that cause directly. Cherrapunji stands on the edge of a plateau that looks over the plains of Bengal. There it catches the full force of the monsoon as the moist air rises from the sea. A good coal seam in the vicinity is the one other fact the entry adds.
britannica-1911-fuji: Fuji, also Fuji-san or Fujiyama, is a celebrated mountain of Japan standing west-south-west of Tokyo, about 70 miles by rail from that city. It rises 12,395 feet, and its southern slopes reach Suruga Bay. It is a cone of simple form, striking because it stands alone. The summit is broken by a crater some 2000 feet across, for Fuji is a quiet volcano. An eruption is recorded as late as the first decade of the 18th century, and pilgrims resort to it in numbers.
britannica-1911-rufiji:
Rufiji is a river article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a large river of German East Africa. It reaches the sea through a broad delta. Its upper basin runs more than three hundred miles from north to south. Three main branches drain that basin and join to form the lower Rufiji.

The two southern branches, the Luvegu and the Ulanga, are shorter than the northern Ruaha. Yet they carry more water, since they come from a more rainy region. Where the Luvegu and Ulanga meet, the Rufiji proper may be said to begin. The Luvegu flows north-east in a wooded valley, mostly narrow. In its lower course it is a broad stream, one hundred to one hundred and fifty yards wide. The Ulanga is formed by streams that fall from a high plateau near Lake Nyasa.
britannica-1911-takhtsingji:
Takhtsingji, Maharaja of Bhaunagar, who lived from 1858 to 1896, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. A Rajput chief of the Gohel clan, he came to the throne in 1870, on his father's death. In his youth the state was run jointly by an English officer and an Indian statesman, while he was schooled at Rajkot.

At twenty he took full rule of a state near 3,000 square miles in size. His first act backed a railway link to a trunk line, a first for a raja in western India. Trade in its wake set him on reform. Schools, hospitals, and roads grew fast, and in 1886 he set up a council of state. He took his attackers to court in Bombay, and in 1893 Cambridge gave him a law degree.
britannica-1911-tata-jamsetji-nasarwanji:
Jamsetji Nasarwanji Tata, who lived from 1839 to 1904, was a Parsee merchant and giver. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica honors his trade and gifts. He was born at Nosari in the state of Baroda. As a boy he moved to Bombay and studied at Elphinstone College.

Tata joined his father firm in 1858 and built cotton mills. Mills at Bombay and Nagpur led to plans for modern iron works. He fought a long fight to cut freight rates to China and Japan. He brought silk making on Japanese lines into Mysore. He also built the Taj Mahal hotel in Bombay. His greatest gift endowed a research school at Bangalore. He died in Germany in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Fiji is a vicariate covering an archipelago of some 250 islands, about ninety inhabited, across 7,435 square miles of the central western Pacific. Discovered by Cook in 1773, little visited until Wesleyan missionaries arrived in 1835, the islands were ceded unconditionally by their chiefs to Britain in 1874 after long internal troubles.

In 1911 the population was 139,541, mostly Fijians, with Europeans, Indians, and other eastern peoples. The Fijians, of Melanesian stock much crossed with Polynesian, held a religion the entry calls ancestor worship, honouring chiefs, heroes. Ancestors as lesser gods still subject to human passions and even death, alongside malicious deities and four classes of gods. Christianity, the entry notes, was rapidly displacing that old religion.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Milit:
In 2017, a United States Navy office that worked on drone warfare raised a string of concerns. The subject was the Defense Department's use of drones sold by DJI, a Chinese company whose small aircraft dominated the commercial market. The document came to the National Security Archive through a Freedom of Information Act request, and the Archive published it in December 2019.

The worry at the heart of the memo is data: what a foreign-made drone collects, where that information goes, and what an adversary could learn from it. Cheap, capable commercial drones had spread through the military faster than security rules could follow. For readers, the release is a neat primary source on a modern problem, the clash between buying the best tool on the market and trusting the country that made it.
peach-blossom-shangri-la-tao-hua-yuan-ji:
Peach Blossom Shangri-la, or Tao Hua Yuan Ji, is the most famous short tale in Chinese literature, written by Tao Yuanming. This edition gives it in English, translated and proofed by Rick Davis and David Steelman, with the Chinese original included. It tells of a fisherman of Wuling in the Jin dynasty.

Following a stream, the fisherman finds a grove of peach trees and a narrow opening in a mountain. Beyond it lies a hidden valley of good fields, ponds, and contented people, cut off from the world for centuries. The tale became China's lasting image of a perfect, unreachable land.
podcast-dannyjones-bT1QPEEIgjI:
Wildlife star Manny Puig returns to Danny Jones to talk sharks and a strange sea. Puig rose to fame on wild television shows handling beasts. His carved tridents sit on display in the studio.

Jones says their first talk covered his rise and animal work. This visit reaches back to his childhood in Cuba. Then the pair turn to odd shark behavior named in the title. Puig speaks as a man who has spent his life in the water. The episode mixes memoir with ocean mystery, told by a handler few can match.
podcast-joerogan-Fafk-6i37jI:
Could human conflict be the reason we have not found alien life? A segment of the Joe Rogan Experience turns that idea over. The puzzle is old: the universe is vast and old, yet the sky stays silent. Rogan tests one answer, that species like ours may wreck themselves first.

The talk moves through war, nukes, and the short fuse of our own history, asking whether other worlds fail the same test. Rogan also weighs quieter options, from distance to simple disinterest. The segment is bar-room philosophy at a cosmic scale, grounded in a real riddle that scientists still argue about.
podcast-joerogan-vzIGGKJCdJI:
Truth itself is the subject of this Joe Rogan Experience clip with Jordan Peterson. Peterson asks what counts as true and who gets to decide in a culture of clashing stories. The short segment distills one of his core lectures into a single exchange.

Peterson argues that truth is more than facts, tying it to how a person should act. He warns that lies, even small ones, bend a life and a society out of shape. Rogan presses him with plain cases and everyday examples. The clip gives new listeners a fast taste of Peterson's heavy but popular style.
